items.zh: 二禪 · 明支義、體用、淺深、進退、功德
parent: The Second Dhyāna: Its Name and Cultivation

zh: 二、明支義者，二禪有四支：一、內淨；二、喜；三、樂；四、一心。今明支義，例有通、別。支持、支離之義，類如前說。一、所言內淨支者，既離覺觀，依內淨心發定，皎潔分明，無有垢穢，故名內淨支。二、喜支者，定與喜俱發，行者深心自慶，於內心生喜、定等十種功德善法故，悅豫無量，故名喜支。三、樂支者，行者受於喜中之樂，恬澹悅怡，綿綿美快，故名樂支。四、一心支者，受樂心息，既不緣定內喜樂，復不緣外念思想，一心不動，故名一心支。
en: Second, clarifying the meaning of the factors: the second dhyāna has four factors — inner purity; joy; happiness; and one-pointedness of mind. Here, the meaning of "factor" is clarified along the same pattern, having both a general and a particular sense — the meanings of "sustaining" and "branching apart" are as already given above.

First, as for the factor of inner purity: having left initial thought and sustained reflection behind, concentration is brought forth in reliance on the inwardly pure mind, radiant and distinct, free of any defilement — hence this is named the factor of inner purity. Second, the factor of joy: concentration arises together with joy, the practitioner deeply celebrating within, the inner mind giving rise to joy, concentration, and the other ten kinds of meritorious, wholesome dharma — delight beyond measure — hence this is named the factor of joy. Third, the factor of happiness: the practitioner receives the happiness present within this joy, tranquil, contented, and continuously delightful — hence this is named the factor of happiness. Fourth, the factor of one-pointedness of mind: the mind of happiness having come to rest, one no longer takes the inward joy and happiness of concentration as an object, nor takes any external thought or deliberation as an object either — the mind one-pointed and unmoving — hence this is named the factor of one-pointedness of mind.

zh: 問曰：《纓絡經》何得於一心前立猗支邪？答曰：猶是內淨，於喜樂後，立異名說。所以者何？猗名為縱，縱名為任，既內無垢累，猗任自在，不慮聲刺及覺觀所牽，故言猗。問曰：《大集經》中何故但立三支，無內淨邪？答曰：彼經以存略不說。二禪名為喜俱定，既離覺觀說喜，必知有內淨定。通、別立支之意，類前可知。三、明體用因果者，如《纓絡經》說二禪四支為因，第五默然心為定體，翻覆明因果體用之義，不異初禪。四、明淺深者，例如初禪，從初品乃至次第發勝品，此為淺深之相，可見，今不別明。第五、明進退之義，例如初禪。六、明功德中，即還為二意：一者、離過德；二者、善心德。故《大集經》云：「二禪者，亦名為離，亦名為具。所言離者，離五蓋；所言具者，謂具四支。」若言離過者，離覺觀過。具者，從內淨喜心具足，生信、敬、慚、愧等及六善法也。
en: Question: how is it that the Yingluo Sūtra establishes a factor of pliancy before one-pointedness of mind? Answer: this is still inner purity, simply given a different name after joy and happiness. Why is this? "Pliancy" means release, and release means ease — since there is, within, no defiling entanglement left at all, one is at ease and free, no longer troubled by sound's own sting or drawn along by initial thought and sustained reflection — hence it is called "pliancy." Question: why does the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra establish only three factors, without inner purity at all? Answer: that sūtra simply retains the essentials and omits the rest. Since the second dhyāna is named the concentration joined with joy, and joy is spoken of precisely because initial thought and sustained reflection have been left behind, the presence of inner-purity concentration is thereby already implied. The sense of the general and particular establishing of factors follows the same pattern as before, and may be understood accordingly.

Third, clarifying substance, function, cause, and effect: as the Yingluo Sūtra says, the second dhyāna's four factors serve as the cause, and the fifth, the mind of silence, serves as the substance of concentration — turning this back and forth to clarify the sense of cause, effect, substance, and function is no different from the first dhyāna. Fourth, clarifying depth: following the same pattern as the first dhyāna, proceeding from the initial grade in sequence to ever more excellent grades — this is the mark of shallowness and depth, which may be readily seen, and is not separately clarified here. Fifth, the sense of progress and regression follows the same pattern as the first dhyāna as well.

Sixth, clarifying merit: this itself again has two parts — the merit of freedom from fault; and the merit of a wholesome mind. Hence the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says: "The second dhyāna is likewise named both 'freedom' and 'completeness.' As for 'freedom': this means freedom from the five hindrances. As for 'completeness': this means completeness in the four factors." As for freedom from fault: this means freedom from the fault of initial thought and sustained reflection. As for completeness: from the inner-purity, joyful mind, complete in itself, faith, reverence, shame, remorse, and the like, together with the six wholesome dharmas, are brought forth.

"Pliancy" (猗) turning out to be inner purity under another name — introduced late in the sequence by one sūtra but absent from another's list entirely — is a good illustration of how this treatise handles cross-textual variation generally: rather than picking one canonical enumeration as correct, it shows how each source's apparent addition or omission still resolves back to the same underlying structure once properly understood. This closes the whole of the second dhyāna.

zh:
次明第三禪相。禪義如偈說：
攝心第一定，寂然無所見。
患苦欲棄之，亦如捨覺觀。
由愛故有苦，失喜則生憂。
離苦樂身安，捨念及方便。
此偈中具明三禪修證之相。今釋三禪義，亦開為三：一者、釋名；二、明修習；三、明得證。第一、釋三禪名者，行者於第三心中得五種支林功德定中之善法，故名三禪也。若依《地持論》，名為樂俱禪，此定功德眷屬與遍身樂俱發故，猶是無覺無觀三昧聖默然定之所攝，但名通。於前二禪中已受名，今不重釋。
en:
Next, clarifying the mark of the third dhyāna. The meaning of this dhyāna, as the verse says:
"Gathering the mind into the foremost concentration, still and seeing nothing at all;
Troubled by suffering, one wishes to abandon it, just as initial thought and sustained reflection were once left behind.
Because of attachment there is suffering; losing joy, sorrow then arises.
Free of suffering, happy, and at bodily ease — with equanimity, mindfulness, and skillful means."
This verse clarifies in full the marks of the third dhyāna's cultivation and realization. Here, the meaning of the third dhyāna is explained, likewise in three parts: explaining the name; clarifying its cultivation; and clarifying its realization.

First, explaining the name of the third dhyāna: the practitioner, at this third stage of mind, attains five kinds of the wholesome dharma of a grove-of-factors' merit within concentration — hence it is named the third dhyāna. According to the Bodhisattva-bhūmi Treatise, it is named the dhyāna joined with happiness, since this concentration's own merit and retinue arise together with happiness pervading the whole body. It, too, still belongs to the samādhi without initial thought or sustained reflection, the concentration of noble silence — this is simply its general name; having already received this name within the second dhyāna above, it is not explained again here.

zh: 第二、釋修習三禪方法，如前一行半偈說：「攝心第一定，寂然無所見。患苦欲棄之，亦如捨覺觀。由愛故有苦，失喜則生憂。」此偈廣說訶二禪喜相。今行者觀二禪為過失，欲得三禪時，是中應具足明六行方法，今但略出二禪過罪相六行之義。此二禪定雖從內淨而發，但大喜勇動，定不牢固，類如前說。但誑心念著安隱處，如人知婦是羅剎女，則棄之，不生戀著，一心專念三禪功德，爾時即捨大喜及與默然。當如上用三法遣之：一、不受；二、訶責；三、觀心窮檢。既不受喜，喜及默然則自謝，三禪未生，中間有定亦如是說，但淺深有異，行者是時慎勿憂悔。過同前說。
en: Second, explaining the method for cultivating the third dhyāna: as the first one and a half verse-lines (each of four phrases) already given above say: "Gathering the mind into the foremost concentration, still and seeing nothing at all; troubled by suffering, one wishes to abandon it, just as initial thought and sustained reflection were once left behind. Because of attachment there is suffering; losing joy, sorrow then arises." This verse explains at length the reproach of the second dhyāna's own mark of joy.

Here, the practitioner, contemplating the second dhyāna as a fault, and wishing to attain the third dhyāna, should, at this point, be complete in the method of the six practices in full; here, only the sense of the second dhyāna's own faulty marks and the six practices are given in brief. Although this second-dhyāna concentration arises through inner purity, its great joy remains excited and stirred, its concentration not yet secure — following the same pattern as already described above. It merely deceives the mind into clinging to it as a place of peace. Like a man who, learning his wife is in truth a rākṣasī, abandons her at once, with no further longing or attachment, one applies the mind single-mindedly to the merit of the third dhyāna, and, at that point, relinquishes both the great joy and silence together. One should use the same three methods as before to dispel it: not receiving it; reproaching it; and contemplating the mind, examining it to its very root. Once joy is no longer received, joy itself, together with silence, passes away of its own accord; and, with the third dhyāna not yet arisen, there is, in the interval, a concentration present here as well, spoken of in the same way, differing only in its own degree of depth — the practitioner, at this point, must take great care not to fall into worry or regret. Its fault is the same as already described above.

The rākṣasī-wife simile is pointed in a way worth sitting with: the second dhyāna's joy is not being denounced as fake or worthless, only recognized as, in the end, dangerous to remain attached to — exactly like a wife genuinely loved who turns out to be something the practitioner cannot safely stay bound to. This is the third time in three dhyānas the treatise has needed a fresh simile for the same basic move (leaving a genuine good behind for a better one), each time landing on something more visceral than the last — the goldsmith's son's return to counting breath, then the three-tiered eviction of an unwanted houseguest, now this.

items.en: The Third Dhyāna: Its Arising and Two Kinds of Happiness
items.zh: 三禪 · 明證相 · 明禪發
parent: The Third Dhyāna: Its Name and Cultivation

zh: 第三、明三禪發相，亦類前為六意：一、正明三禪發相；二、明支義；三、明因果；四、明淺深；五、明進退；六、明功德。第一、明三禪發相者，加功不止，一心修習，其心湛然安靜，爾時樂定未發，而不加功力，心自澄靜，即是三禪未到地。於後其心泯然入定，不依內外，與樂俱發。當樂發時，亦有功德眷屬，具如前辨，但無動勇之喜為異，而綿綿之樂從內心而發，心樂美妙，不可為喻。
en: Third, clarifying the mark of the third dhyāna's own arising: this, too, follows the same pattern as before, in six parts — directly clarifying the mark of the third dhyāna's own arising; clarifying the meaning of its factors; clarifying its cause and effect; clarifying its depth; clarifying its progress and regression; and clarifying its merits.

First, clarifying the mark of the third dhyāna's own arising: applying effort without ceasing, cultivating single-mindedly, the mind grows deep and tranquil; at this point, the concentration of happiness has not yet arisen, and yet, without any further application of effort, the mind grows calm and still of its own accord — this is precisely the third dhyāna's own "not-yet-arrived" state. Afterward, the mind enters concentration indistinctly, relying neither on what is within nor without, arising together with happiness. At the very moment this happiness arises, it, too, has its own retinue of merit, exactly as already distinguished above, differing only in having no excited, leaping joy present; and this continuous happiness arises from the inner mind itself, the mind's own happiness wondrous and fine, beyond any comparison.

zh: 樂定初生，既未即遍身，中間多有三過：一者、樂定既淺，其心沈沒，少有智慧用；二者、樂定微少，心智勇發，故不安隱；三者、樂定之心與慧力等，綿綿美妙，多生貪著，其心迷醉。故經言：「是樂聖人得捨，餘人捨為難。」三禪欲發，有此三過，則樂定不得增長遍身，行者當善調適。云何調適？當用三法：一者、心若沈沒，當用念、精進、慧等法策起；二者、若心勇發，當念三昧定法攝之；三者、心若迷醉，當念後樂及諸勝妙法門，以自醒悟，令心不著。行者若能善修三法，調適樂定，當知樂法必定增長，遍滿身分，是故經言：「三禪受遍身樂。」
en: When the concentration of happiness first arises, it is not yet spread through the whole body, and, in the interval, there are commonly three faults present: first, the concentration of happiness being still shallow, the mind sinks down, with little use of wisdom present; second, the concentration of happiness being still slight, the mind and intellect become excitedly stirred, and so it is not yet at peace; and third, the mind of this concentration of happiness, now equal in strength to the power of wisdom, being continuous and wondrous, gives rise, for the most part, to craving and attachment, the mind growing intoxicated by it. Hence the sūtra says: "This happiness is something the noble ones are able to relinquish; for everyone else, relinquishing it is difficult." As the third dhyāna is about to arise, these three faults are present, and so the concentration of happiness is unable to grow and spread through the whole body — the practitioner should properly regulate and adjust it.

How does one regulate it? One should use three methods: first, if the mind sinks down, one should rouse it up using mindfulness, diligence, wisdom, and other such dharmas; second, if the mind becomes excitedly stirred, one should hold it in check by recollecting the dharma of samādhi-concentration; and third, if the mind grows intoxicated, one should recollect the happiness yet to come and the other excellent, wondrous dharma-gates, to awaken oneself, so that the mind does not become attached. If the practitioner is able to skillfully cultivate these three methods, regulating and adjusting the concentration of happiness, one should know that the dharma of happiness is bound to grow and spread throughout the entire body — hence the sūtra says: "The third dhyāna receives happiness pervading the whole body."

zh: 問曰：若樂充滿遍身，身具五根，五根之中，悉有樂不？答：樂遍身時，身諸毛孔悉皆欣悅。爾時五情雖無外塵發識，而樂法內出，充滿諸根，五根之中，皆悉悅樂，但無外塵對，則不發五識。情依於身，身樂既滿，情得通悅，樂與意識相應，以識內滿故，則遍身而受，所以佛說三禪之樂遍身而受。復次，初禪樂從外而發，外識相應，意識不相應，內樂不滿；二禪之樂雖從內發，然從喜而生，喜根相應，樂根不相應，樂依於喜，喜尚不遍，況於樂邪？今三禪之樂從內發，以樂為主，內無喜動，念慧因緣，令樂增長遍身，內外充滿，恬愉快樂，世間第一樂中之上，故佛說行慈果報遍淨地中。
en: Question: if happiness fills the whole body, and the body possesses five faculties, is happiness present within each of the five faculties as well? Answer: when happiness pervades the whole body, every pore of the body is filled with delight. At that time, although the five faculties of feeling give rise to no consciousness through any external sense-object, the dharma of happiness issues forth from within, filling every faculty completely — within each of the five faculties, delight and happiness are present throughout; it is simply that, with no external object present to correspond to, none of the five sense-consciousnesses is thereby brought forth. The faculties of feeling depend upon the body, and, the body's happiness now complete, the faculties of feeling, too, become thoroughly delighted, this happiness corresponding with mind-consciousness — and, because consciousness itself is filled from within, happiness is thus received throughout the whole body; hence the Buddha says that the third dhyāna's happiness is received throughout the entire body.

Furthermore: the first dhyāna's happiness arises from without, corresponding with the outer consciousnesses but not with mind-consciousness, and so its inner happiness is not yet complete. The second dhyāna's happiness, although it arises from within, nonetheless arises from joy, corresponding with the joy-faculty but not with the happiness-faculty — happiness there still depends upon joy, and, since even joy itself is not yet pervasive, how much less could happiness be? Here, the third dhyāna's happiness arises from within, with happiness itself as the ruling factor, no excited joy present within it at all; through the causes and conditions of mindfulness and wisdom, happiness is made to grow and spread throughout the whole body, filling both within and without, tranquil and delightful — the very foremost and highest of every worldly happiness. Hence the Buddha says that the karmic result of practicing loving-kindness lies within the ground of universal purity.

zh: 問曰：佛說三禪有二時樂：一、受樂；二、快樂。約何義說邪？答曰：實爾。快樂樂者，樂定初發，未遍身也。受樂樂者，樂既增長，遍身受。譬如石中之泉，從內涌出，盈流於外，遍滿溝渠。三禪之樂亦復如是。
en: Question: the Buddha speaks of the third dhyāna as having happiness at two distinct times: received happiness; and immediate happiness — with reference to what sense is this spoken of? Answer: this is indeed so. As for immediate happiness: this is the concentration of happiness at its first arising, not yet spread throughout the body. As for received happiness: this is once happiness has already grown and is received throughout the whole body. It is like a spring within rock, gushing forth from within and overflowing outward, filling every channel and ditch completely — the happiness of the third dhyāna is exactly the same.

The three faults during happiness's initial, unstable phase (sinking, excited overshoot, intoxicated attachment) map onto exactly the three regulatory tools given as their antidotes — rousing energy for the first, calming recollection for the second, and reflective perspective for the third — the same "matched antidote" logic from fascicle 4's treatment of unwholesome roots, now applied to managing a wholesome state rather than curing an unwholesome one. The claim that third-dhyāna happiness reaches all five sense-faculties without any of the five sense-consciousnesses actually firing is a genuinely careful psychological distinction: bodily delight can saturate the sensory system directly, from within, without needing any external stimulus to trigger it — which is precisely what makes it categorically different from ordinary sensory pleasure.

quiz.q: What are the second dhyāna's four factors?
quiz.why: "The second dhyāna has four factors — inner purity; joy; happiness; and one-pointedness of mind."

quiz.q: The Yingluo Sūtra places a factor of pliancy before one-pointedness. How does the text explain it?
options: it is still inner purity, renamed after joy and happiness; pliancy means release and ease, free of defilement and not drawn by thought
quiz.why: "This is still inner purity, simply given a different name after joy and happiness. Why is this? 'Pliancy' means release, and release means ease — since there is, within, no defiling entanglement left at all, one is at ease and free."

quiz.q: Why does the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra list only three factors for the second dhyāna, without inner purity?
options: that sūtra simply abbreviates; since joy is spoken of after leaving thought and reflection, inner purity is implied
quiz.why: "That sūtra simply retains the essentials and omits the rest. Since the second dhyāna is named the concentration joined with joy, and joy is spoken of precisely because initial thought and sustained reflection have been left behind, the presence of inner-purity concentration is thereby already implied."

quiz.q: What fault does the second dhyāna's merit of freedom from fault remove?
options: the fault of initial thought and sustained reflection
quiz.why: "As for freedom from fault: this means freedom from the fault of initial thought and sustained reflection." The third dhyāna alone is free of joy's fault, and the fourth of sorrow, joy, suffering, and happiness.

quiz.q: According to the Bodhisattva-bhūmi, what is the third dhyāna called, and why?
options: the dhyāna joined with happiness, since its merits arise with happiness pervading the body
quiz.why: "According to the Bodhisattva-bhūmi Treatise, it is named the dhyāna joined with happiness, since this concentration's own merit and retinue arise together with happiness pervading the whole body."

quiz.q: What simile illustrates relinquishing the second dhyāna's great joy?
options: like a man who learns his wife is a rākṣasī and abandons her without longing
quiz.why: "Like a man who, learning his wife is in truth a rākṣasī, abandons her at once, with no further longing or attachment — one applies the mind single-mindedly to the merit of the third dhyāna, and, at that point, relinquishes both the great joy and noble silence together."

quiz.q: Which three methods dispel the second dhyāna's joy?
options: not receiving, reproaching, examining the mind to its root
quiz.why: "One should use the same three methods as before to dispel it: not receiving it; reproaching it; and contemplating the mind, examining it to its very root. Once joy is no longer received, joy itself, together with noble silence, passes away of its own accord."

quiz.q: Why must the second dhyāna be relinquished?
options: though born of inner purity, its great joy is excited and the concentration not secure
quiz.why: "Although this second-dhyāna concentration arises through inner purity, its great joy remains excited and stirred, its concentration not yet secure." The second dhyāna has already left thought behind; the problem is joy.

quiz.q: How does the arising of the third dhyāna's happiness differ from what came before?
options: no excited, leaping joy; a continuous happiness from the inner mind
quiz.why: "At the very moment this happiness arises, it, too, has its own retinue of merit ... differing only in having no excited, leaping joy present; and this continuous happiness arises from the inner mind itself." The breath ceasing belongs to the fourth dhyāna.

quiz.q: How is each of the three faults regulated?
options: sinking: rouse with mindfulness, diligence, wisdom; excitement: restrain by recollecting samādhi; intoxication: recollect later happiness and higher gates to wake oneself
quiz.why: "First, if the mind sinks down, one should rouse it up using mindfulness, diligence, wisdom, and other such dharmas; second, if the mind becomes excitedly stirred, one should hold it in check by recollecting the dharma of samādhi-concentration; and third, if the mind grows intoxicated, one should recollect the happiness yet to come and the other excellent, wondrous dharma-gates."

quiz.q: When happiness pervades the body, is it in all five faculties, and why do no sense-consciousnesses arise?
options: all five are delighted, but with no outer object no sense-consciousness arises; the happiness corresponds with mind-consciousness, filling it, so it is felt throughout
quiz.why: "Although the five faculties of feeling give rise to no consciousness through any external sense-object, the dharma of happiness issues forth from within, filling every faculty completely ... it is simply that, with no external object present to correspond to, none of the five sense-consciousnesses is thereby brought forth."

quiz.q: What are the third dhyāna's "two times of happiness," and what simile illustrates them?
options: immediate happiness at first arising, not yet pervasive; received happiness when it pervades the body — like a spring welling from rock and filling the channels
quiz.why: "As for immediate happiness: this is the concentration of happiness at its first arising, not yet spread throughout the body. As for received happiness: this is once happiness has already grown and is received throughout the whole body. It is like a spring within rock, gushing forth from within and overflowing outward."

quiz.q: How does the text compare the happiness of the first, second, and third dhyānas?
options: the first's arises from without with outer consciousness; the second's from within but depends on joy; the third's from within with happiness itself as ruler, filling the body — the foremost worldly happiness
quiz.why: "The first dhyāna's happiness arises from without ... The second dhyāna's happiness, although it arises from within, nonetheless arises from joy ... Here, the third dhyāna's happiness arises from within, with happiness itself as the ruling factor ... the very foremost and highest of every worldly happiness."
